title: Endianness and Alignment
subtitle: How bytes sit in memory — and why struct {char; int;} is not 5 bytes.
summary: See little vs big endian, network order, and the padding rules that decide struct layout and size.
learning_objectives: Predict memory byte order for a 32-bit integer on little vs big endian.
Use htonl/ntohl correctly and explain why networking needs it.
Explain why padding exists, compute sizeof and offsetof, and fix layout with reordering or alignas.

blocks.title: Memory is just bytes
blocks.markdown: A `uint32_t 0x01020304` is four bytes. The machine must pick an order to store them. Your laptop (x64, ARM default) picks little-endian: `04 03 02 01` in RAM. The network picks big-endian: `01 02 03 04` on the wire. Every `struct` is this idea plus alignment.

Write a 4-byte value, dump it with a hex tool or by casting to bytes. The order you see in RAM is the machine's endianness. The value as an integer is the same; the bytes in memory are reversed between the two conventions.

Networking code always converts with `htonl` / `ntohl` so peers agree. Skipping the call is the classic bug that works on one machine and fails on another.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing 0x01020304 stored as 01 02 03 04 on big-endian and 04 03 02 01 on little-endian.
blocks.caption: Same value, different byte order in memory. Network order is big-endian by definition.

blocks.explanation: Casts the integer's address to bytes and prints them. On little-endian you see 04 03 02 01; swap the bytes and print again to show the conversion.

blocks.markdown:
CPUs prefer aligned access: a 4-byte `int` wants address % 4 == 0, an 8-byte pointer wants % 8. The compiler inserts unnamed padding bytes so every member is aligned. `struct { char a; int b; }` has 1 byte for `a`, 3 bytes of padding, then 4 bytes for `b` → 8 bytes total. Put the big member first and you save the padding.

`sizeof` includes padding. `offsetof` tells you where each member sits. `alignas` forces a stricter alignment (for example 64 to avoid false sharing on a cache line).

blocks.explanation: Prints size, padding and offset. Swapping member order shows how layout affects size. Visualise with web/assets diagrams or your own drawings.
blocks.expected_output: A 8 ... B 8 (but packing differs; try char; char; int etc.)

blocks.title: C language — offsetof and alignas
blocks.purpose: Check padding, alignment and offsetof guarantees before trusting folklore.

blocks.question: On a little-endian machine, struct {char a; int b;} with a=0x11, b=0x01020304 will most likely occupy how many bytes and what byte sequence starts the struct?
blocks.explanation: Padding inserts 3 bytes after a so that b starts at an aligned offset. b itself is stored little-endian: 04 03 02 01.

blocks.title: Shrink a struct
blocks.objective: Reorder members and measure sizeof / offsetof.
instructions: Create struct D with members char, double, char, int.
Print sizeof and offsetof for each member.
Reorder members by descending alignment (double → int → char) and re-measure.
Try __attribute__((packed)) or #pragma pack(1) and reason why production code rarely uses them.
hints: double wants 8-byte alignment; char wants 1. Sorting biggest first minimises holes.
completion_criteria: You report original and reordered sizes with an explanation
You state where padding bytes sit
